cards.title: Test letters and follow-ups with actual returns before full send
cards.summary: Keyed split tests across many letter variants pick the winner that gets the most responses, mirroring scientific ad testing.
cards.use_when: Running an email or direct-mail campaign (abandoned cart, replenishment reminder, win-back) and deciding which message to scale.
steps: Before sending millions of pieces, build a small test: the source publisher tries up to 25 letter variants, each mailed to about 1,000 prospects.
Key each variant so responses are traceable, then compare cost-per-result, not just open or reply counts.
Compute what results will cost; if the best variant appears unprofitable, abandon the plan rather than scaling a loser.
Roll out only the variant that pays best on actual returns.
For ecommerce: apply the same discipline to abandoned-cart, post-purchase, and replenishment flows — write several subject/body/offer variants, split a sample of the list, and scale the winner.
caveats: The source's 25-variant/1,000-prospect scale is a mail-order example, not a required benchmark; adapt sample size to your list and traffic.
Test where possible; where not possible, base the message on knowledge gained from prior tests.

cards.title: Follow up inquirers along the original interest, not a new argument
cards.summary: A follow-up letter should complete the impression the prospect already formed, not restart with a different pitch.
cards.use_when: Writing follow-up emails to leads who requested a quote, sample, catalog, or signed up but did not buy.
steps: Identify what created the original interest (the ad, offer, or page that captured the lead).
Continue that same argument and promise in the follow-up — do not introduce a different selling angle or guess again.
Note which selling letters add urgency: a limit on the offer, an expiry date, or a stated cost of delay.
Add a specific inducement for immediate action rather than generic 'act now' language.
For ecommerce: if a lead downloaded a size guide, follow up on fit and selection rather than switching to a price/discount pitch unless price was the original hook.
caveats: Follow-up letters go to 'half-made converts,' so they are high-leverage; the wrong argument forfeits the impression already gained.
Offers must expire on a genuine date — the source's point is to force prompt decision, not to fake scarcity.

cards.title: Give a compelling personal reason to order from you rather than a competitor's catalog
cards.summary: A gift or personal note enclosed with the catalog gives the buyer a reason to order from this vendor instead of the several competitors he also requested.
cards.use_when: Fulfilling catalog or sample requests in a category where buyers request multiple competing catalogs.
steps: Recognize the competition: an inquirer may send for three or four similar catalogs, so your catalog alone does not win the order.
Enclose a letter and a personal card with the catalog. Say you are a new customer and want to welcome them.
Ask them to enclose the card with their order so you can guarantee a gift — something they keep.
Differentiate the reason for old customers versus new customers (e.g., a different justification for the same gift).
Measure whether the gift pays for itself through larger sales per catalog; the source reports it paid several times over, so treat as an example to verify, not a promise.
caveats: The gift's payback is a reported case result, not a guaranteed outcome.
The curiosity the offer arouses must favor your catalog over alternatives; a weak reason will not beat a competing offer.

cards.title: Price prompt action into your offer rather than losing to delay
cards.summary: You can afford to pay for immediate action; delay costs more than the inducement.
cards.use_when: Setting promotional mechanics (expiry windows, premiums, bundles) for a product launch or seasonal push.
steps: Strike while the iron is hot: ask for the decision at the moment of interest.
Offer an inducement for prompt action, or state what delay will cost the buyer.
Consider time-limited mechanics: the source cites an advertiser who got hundreds of thousands of women to buy six packages and send trademarks for a premium good for only one week.
Evaluate whether the premium or discount cost is less than the value of accelerated purchases and reduced delay.
For ecommerce: test expiring bundles or first-order premiums at checkout rather than always-on discounts.
caveats: The six-package/trademark/week-long premium is a case example, not a universal template.
The source warns no single tactic applies to two lines — ways of getting action are many, but principles are universal; test for your category.

cards.title: Choose product names that either tell a selling story or accept a long earned-meaning path
cards.summary: A name displayed prominently should aid advertising; descriptive names do, meaningless coined names only pay off after long advertising.
cards.use_when: Naming a new product, bundle, or house brand where the name will be displayed in ads and on listings.
steps: Classify your candidate name: descriptive (May Breath, Cream of Wheat, Dutch Cleanser, Holeproof, Minute Tapioca) versus meaningless coinage (Kodak, Karo, Vaseline, Kotex, Lux, Postum).
If descriptive, note it can be both protected and self-explanatory, so display space earns its keep.
If coined, accept that the great majority of coined names never attain meaning; do not assume yours will.
Avoid names that consist of common descriptive ingredients (Syrup of Figs, Coconut Oil Shampoo, Tar Soap) — they invite substitution, force you into a comparison class, and cap pricing power.
Avoid unfortunate generic names (Toasted Corn Flakes, Malted Milk) where creating demand also creates demand for competitors using the same words.
Avoid frivolous coinages for a serious product; the source says frivolity almost prohibits respect.
caveats: Names have lost originators 'four-fifths of the trade they developed' in the source's examples — but these are historical cases, not predicted outcomes for your name.
On patented products, the right to a name expires with the patent (Castoria, Aspirin, Shredded Wheat Biscuit), so patent protection can itself be undesirable.

cards.title: When a common name is unavoidable, use the founder's name
cards.summary: A man's name as an auxiliary brand is better than a coined name because it signals personal pride in the product.
cards.use_when: Naming a product whose category term must be a common name (e.g., you must call it 'soap' or 'oil').
steps: Accept that the generic product word cannot be owned or protected.
Add a man's name as the auxiliary brand — the source says this is much better than a coined name because it shows someone is proud of his creation.
Recognize this naming decision as foundational: some names became the chief factors in success, others lost four-fifths of the trade their originators developed.
Display the name so it supplements, not replaces, the selling story; the service of the product, not the name, is the important thing.
caveats: The four-fifths figure is a historical example, not a benchmark.
The source's advice is directional and dated in its gender framing; the transferable principle is that an eponymous brand implies personal accountability.

cards.title: Eliminate wasted ad display space telling no selling story
cards.summary: A vast amount of space is wasted displaying names and pictures that tell no selling story; modern advertising moves to cut that waste.
cards.use_when: Auditing ad creative or PDP hero modules where brand marks, logos, or decorative images occupy prime real estate.
steps: Tally how much of each ad or page is spent on name, logo, or decorative imagery versus selling content.
For each element, ask whether it advances the selling story; if not, cut or compress it.
Justify prominent name display only when the name itself aids advertising (descriptive names earn this; meaningless coinages do not).
For ecommerce: reduce oversized brand imagery on PDPs and ads unless it carries product information (ingredients, use case, proof).
caveats: The source is addressing print advertising; the ecommerce adaptation (PDP, thumbnails) is an analogy, not a documented result.
A strong, established brand can carry display value the source's era could not measure; test before stripping brand assets.

cards.title: Key every ad so results can be known and proved
cards.summary: Ads that are unkeyed are spent blindly; the source argues you can prove an unprofitable ad's worthlessness with a simple keyed test.
cards.use_when: Setting up spend for any paid channel, landing page, or campaign where you cannot yet say whether it pays.
steps: Attach a key: a code, dedicated URL, offer, phone line, or unique ask that ties responses to a specific ad.
Stop running ads you know to be unprofitable, even if they have run for years — cost of a dollar doing a five-dollar job is waste.
Watch for the tell of unkeyed ads: frivolity, clever conceits, entertainment, and palaver a salesman could never say.
The source's blunt test: end an ad with an offer to pay five dollars to anyone who writes that they read it through; the scarcity of replies reveals how few actually read it.
Note that many unkeyed ads today were keyed at the beginning — they won on a small scale before ever running large scale.
caveats: The $5 read-through test is the source's illustrative device, not a recommended offer today; the principle is to build a measurable response key.
Keying measures response, not full attribution; combination effects in growing businesses can still leave advertising's share uncertain.

cards.title: Judge ads by traced returns, not by whether you personally like them
cards.summary: Ads that look crowded or verbose to an admirer may be the top payers; the type with the best traced performance is the one to run.
cards.use_when: Deciding which creative or page style to scale when stakeholders have aesthetic preferences.
steps: Separate the roles: you may be seeking something to admire or entertain, but the buyer is seeking information to act on.
Check whether the ad is keyed; if keyed and among scores of traced ads, the style you dislike may be the best performer.
Let keyed returns, not taste, choose between a 'clean' ad and a dense/informational one.
Keep long-used unkeyed ads suspect; they may simply never have been tested.
For ecommerce: resist replacing a converting PDP because it looks cluttered until a keyed split test proves the new one wins.
caveats: This does not mean density always wins; the source's claim is that traced results should decide, not aesthetics.
Test infrastructure must be reliable or the comparison is meaningless.

cards.title: Apply the storekeeper's discipline to national-scale spend
cards.summary: A storekeeper charges every line of an ad to a department and every inch must justify its cost next day; most national advertising is done without that justification.
cards.use_when: Allocating budget across product lines, departments, or channels where spend is currently credited only by overall business growth.
steps: Charge each line of your ad or campaign to the proper department/product — mirror the storekeeper who must justify every inch the next day.
Require each spend to justify its cost rather than presuming it pays because the business is growing.
Beware crediting advertising for growth from combined efforts: the source cites a $700,000/year advertiser who did not know if advertising was worth anything.
Move to 'safe and sure' small expenditures on known returns that can grow into big ones on a certainty rather than a guess.
For ecommerce: assign channel and campaign budgets to gross margin by product line and review cost per result, not blended revenue growth.
caveats: Combined effects make pure attribution hard; the source's answer is keying and small-scale proof, not perfect multi-touch attribution.
The $700,000 figure is a historical example of an unaware advertiser, not a threshold.

cards.title: Treat advertising as a gamble to be removed, not a tonic to endorse
cards.summary: Spending because advertising worked for others is like taking a secret tonic on endorsement; if the business thrives, the tonic gets credit regardless.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether to launch or continue a paid channel because competitors or past results suggest it 'must' work.
steps: Identify whether current spend is justified by measured return or by presumption and others' endorsements.
If the business thrives, check that you are not simply crediting the tonic; if it fails, do not attribute it to fate.
Replace endorsement reasoning with a test: run a small, keyed campaign and measure cost per result before scaling.
Adopt the source's forecast that advertisers will be judged on known returns and only competent men survive — build the measurement habit before it is forced on you.
For ecommerce: apply this to new channel launches (a paid channel, an affiliate, a marketplace) with a defined test budget and kill criteria.
caveats: This is the source's argument and forecast, not an observed law; some brand advertising intentionally has delayed, hard-to-key effects.
Small tests may not capture long-horizon brand effects — note the limitation when deciding whether to abandon.

cards.title: Win on a small scale before running on a large scale
cards.summary: Ads based on known statistics were keyed at the start and proved themselves at small scale before big rollout.
cards.use_when: Planning a product launch or campaign scale-up where you want evidence before committing large circulation or spend.
steps: Key the ad or campaign at the outset so results are attributable.
Prove the concept at small scale with actual returns.
Only then scale circulation or budget, using the winning variant.
Keep the keying discipline even after scaling to maintain known statistics.
For ecommerce: pilot a new product or creative on a small budget/audience, then expand based on measured cost per result; the source's 'millions of circulation' is the print-era analogy.
caveats: Scale itself can change results (auction dynamics, audience saturation); the source assumes the small-test winner holds up.
Not every product or channel permits small-scale testing — newsletters and follow-ups may have to rely on prior test knowledge instead.

cards.title: Test follow-up sequences because they complete or forfeit the sale
cards.summary: Letters to inquirers and follow-up letters show the same differences as ads — some get action, some complete a sale, some forfeit the impression gained.
cards.use_when: Designing post-inquiry sequences (samples, quotes, cart abandonment) where the first contact only half-converted the buyer.
steps: Recognize follow-ups go to half-made converts, making them disproportionately important relative to their volume.
Where possible, test follow-up letters against each other with keyed responses; where not, base them on knowledge from past tests.
Check each letter for whether it completes the impression already gained or forfeits it.
Ensure the sequence drives toward immediate action via an inducement or a stated cost of delay.
For ecommerce: treat abandoned-cart and post-sample flows as testable creative, not boilerplate — split variants and measure completed-purchase rate.
caveats: The source treats follow-up importance as a general principle; it does not provide sequence-length or timing benchmarks.
Where testing is impossible (low volume), fall back on tested principles rather than inventing a new argument.

cards.title: Match offer mechanics to the line, but keep the universal principles
cards.summary: Ways of getting action are many and rarely transfer directly between lines, but the underlying principles are universal.
cards.use_when: Adapting a proven promotion, premium, or urgency tactic from another category to your own product.
steps: Identify the principle behind a tactic (prompt decision, overcome delay, preference over substitutes) rather than copying the mechanic.
Do not assume one way of getting action applies to two lines; the source says rarely can one way be applied to two lines.
Design a category-appropriate mechanic that serves the same principle, then test it.
Consider that demand you create can be shared by competitors if your name or product term is generic — build a reason to buy from you specifically.
For ecommerce: a time-limited premium that worked in one vertical may need a different mechanic in another; validate before scaling.
caveats: The source is explicit that this is its view, not a tested universal mechanic; treat transfer as a hypothesis.
Descriptive names create category demand that other sellers can also capture, so pair naming with a distinct reason to choose you.

A general letter is never used until it proves itself best among many actual returns. – 57 – Letter writing has much to do with advertising. Letters to inquirers, follow-up letters. Wherever possible they should be tested. Where that is not possible, they should be based on knowledge gained by tests. We find the same difference in letters as in ads. Some get action, some do not. Some complete a sale, some forfeit the impression gained. These are letters, going usually to half-made converts, that are tremendously important.

 Experience generally shows that a two-cent letter gets no more attention than a one-cent letter. Fine stationery no more than poor stationery. The whole appeal lies in the matter. A letter which goes to an inquirer is like a salesman going to an interested prospect. You know what created that interest. Then follow it up along that line, not on some different argument. Complete the impression already created. Don’t undertake another guess. Do something if possible to get immediate action. Offer some inducement for it. Or tell what delay may cost. Note how many successful selling letters place a limit on an offer. It expires on a certain date. That is all done to get prompt decision, to overcome the tendency to delay. A mail order advertiser offered a catalog. The inquirer might send for three or four similar catalogs. He had that competition in making a sale. So he wrote a letter when he sent his catalog, and enclosed a personal card. He said, “You are a new customer, and we want to make you welcome. So when you send your order please enclose this card. The writer wants to see that you get a gift with order — something you can keep.” With an old customer he gave some other reason for the gift. The offer aroused curiosity. It gave preference to his catalog. Without some compelling reason for ordering elsewhere, the woman sent the order to him. The gift paid for itself several times over by bringing larger sales per catalog. The ways for getting action are many. Rarely can one way be applied to two lines. But the principles are universal. Strike while the iron is hot. Get a decision then. Have it followed by prompt action when you can. You can afford to pay for prompt action rather than lose by delay. One advertiser induced hundreds of thousands of women to buy six packages of his product and send him the trademarks, to secure a premium offer good only for one week. – 58 – Chapter 20 A Name That Helps There is great advantage in a name that tells a story. The name is usually prominently displayed. To justify the space it occupies, it should aid the advertising. Some such names are almost complete advertisements in themselves. May Breath is such a name. Cream of Wheat is another. That name alone has been worth a fortune. Other examples are Dutch Cleanser, Cuticura, Dynashine, Minute Tapioca, 3-in-One Oil, Holeproof, Alcorub, etc. Such names may be protected, yet the name itself describes the product, so it makes a valuable display. Other coined names are meaningless. Some examples are Kodak, Karo, Sapolio, Vaseline, Kotex, Lux, Postum, etc. They can be protected, and long-continued advertising may give them a meaning. When this is accomplished they become very valuable. But the great majority of them never attain status. Such names do not aid the advertising. It is very doubtful that they justify display. The service of the product, not the name, is the important thing in advertising. A vast amount of space is wasted in displaying names and pictures which tell no selling story. The tendency of modern advertising is to eliminate waste. Other coined names signify ingredients which anyone may use. Examples are Syrup of Figs, Coconut Oil Shampoo, Tar Soap, Palmolive Soap, etc. Such products may dominate a market if the price is reasonable, but they must to a degree meet competition. They invite substitution. They are naturally classified with other products which have like ingredients, so the price must remain in that class. Toasted Corn Flakes and Malted Milk are examples of unfortunate names. In each of those cases one advertiser created a new demand. When the demand was created, others shared it because they could use the name. The originators depended only on a brand. It is interesting to speculate on how much more profitable a coined name might have been. – 59 – On a patented product it must be remembered that the right to a name expires with that patent. Names like Castoria, Aspirin, Shredded Wheat Biscuit, etc., have become common property. This is a very serious point to consider. It often makes a patent an undesirable protection. Another serious fault in coined names is frivolity. In seeking uniqueness one gets something trivial. And that is a fatal handicap in a serious product. It almost prohibits respect. When a product must be called by a common name, the best auxiliary name is a man’s name. It is much better than a coined name, for it shows that some man is proud of his creation. Thus the question of a name is of serious importance in laying the foundations of a new undertaking. Some names have become the chief factors in success. Some have lost for their originators four-fifths of the trade they developed. – 60 – Chapter 21 Good Business A rapid stream ran by the writer’s boyhood home. The stream turned a wooden wheel and the wheel ran a mill. Under that primitive method, all but a fraction of the streams potentiality went to waste. Then someone applied scientific methods to that stream — put in a turbine and dynamos. Now, with no more water, no more power, it runs a large manufacturing plant. We think of that stream when we see wasted advertising power. And we see it everywhere — hundreds of examples. Enormous potentialities — millions of circulation — used to turn a mill wheel. While others use that same power with manifold effect. We see countless ads running year after year which we know to be unprofitable. Men spending five dollars to do what one dollar might do. Men getting back 30 percent of their cost when they might get 150 percent. And the facts could be easily proved. We see wasted space, frivolity, clever conceits, entertainment. Costly pages filled with palaver which, if employed by a salesman, would reflect on his sanity. But those ads are always unkeyed. The money is spent blindly, merely to satisfy some advertising whim. Not new advertisers only. Many an old advertiser has little or no idea of his advertising results. The business is growing through many efforts combined, and advertising is given its share of the credit. An advertiser of many years standing, spending as high as $700,000 per year, told the writer he did not know whether his advertising was worth anything or not. Sometimes he thought that his business would be just as large without it. The writer replied, “I do know. Your advertising is utterly unprofitable, and I could prove it to you next week. End an ad with an offer to pay five dollars to anyone who writes you that he read the ad through. The scarcity of replies will amaze you.” Think what a confession — that millions of dollars being spent without knowledge of results. Such a policy applied to all factors in a business would bring ruin in short order. You see other ads which you may not like as well. They may seem crowded or verbose. They are not attractive to you, for you are seeking something to admire, – 61 – something to entertain. But you will note that those ads are keyed. The probability is that out of scores of traced ads the type which you see has paid the best. Many other ads which are not keyed now were keyed at the beginning. They are based on known statistics. They won on a small scale before they ever ran on large scale. Those advertisers are utilizing their enormous powers in full. Advertising is prima facie evidence that the man who pays believes that advertising is good. It has brought great results to others, it must be good for him. So he takes it like some secret tonic which others have endorsed. If the business thrives, the tonic gets credit. Otherwise, the failure is due to fate. That seems almost unbelievable. Even a storekeeper who inserts a twenty-dollar ad knows whether it pays or not. Every line of a big store’s ad is charged to the proper department. And every inch used must the next day justify its cost. Yet most national advertising is done without justification. It is merely presumed to pay. A little test might show a way to multiply returns. Such methods, still so prevalent, are not very far from their end. The advertising men who practice them see the writing on the wall. The time is fast coming when men who spend money are going to know what they get. Good business and efficiency will be applied to advertising. Men and methods will be measured by the known returns, and only competent men can survive. Only one hour ago an old advertising man said to the writer, “The day for our type is done. Bunk has lost its power. Sophistry is being displaced by actuality. And I tremble at the trend.” So do hundreds tremble. Enormous advertising is being done along scientific lines. Its success is common knowledge. Advertisers along other lines will not much longer be content. We who can meet the test welcome these changed conditions. Advertisers will multiply when they see that advertising can be safe and sure. Small expenditures made on a guess will grow to big ones on a certainty. Our line of business will be finer, cleaner, when the gamble is removed. And we shall be prouder of it when we are judged on merit.
